coachingPoints: Show players their shooting percentages by zone — data changes habits faster than lectures.
Praise a passed-up bad shot as loudly as a made good one.
Define "your shot" for each player so everyone knows their green lights.
Drill the kick-out and extra pass to manufacture the shots you want, not just hope for them.
commonMistakes: Confusing a make with a good shot — "it went in, so it was fine" is flawed logic.
Taking contested long twos early in the shot clock.
Shooting off balance because the player feels "due" for a make.
Passing up an open three to dribble into traffic.
description: Learn what makes a shot good or bad — it's not just makes and misses. Build a shot diet of layups, free throws, and open threes.
gameSituations: Transition: choosing between an open corner three and a contested layup.
Late clock: taking the best available shot with 5 seconds left.
After an offensive rebound: kicking out for a clean look versus forcing it back up.

howTo.detail: Shots at the rim and open threes are the most efficient shots in basketball; contested long twos are the least. Build your game around the first two and eliminate the third.
howTo.title: Learn the shot spectrum

howTo.detail: Open, on balance, in rhythm — if all three are true, shoot with full confidence. If two are missing, it is probably someone else's shot.
howTo.title: Ask three questions

howTo.detail: If your good shot can become a teammate's great shot with one pass, make the pass. Good teams turn good shots into great ones.
howTo.title: Pass up good for great

howTo.detail: Track where you shoot best and hunt those areas within the offense. Every player has zones — know yours and live in them.
howTo.title: Know your spots

howTo.detail: Early in the clock, only take great shots. Late in the clock, take the best available one. The clock changes what "good" means.
howTo.title: Respect the clock

howTo.detail: Percentages reward patience. A missed open three is still the right shot — keep taking good ones and the math works out over time.
howTo.title: Never let a miss change the math

title: Shot Selection
whatIsIt: Shot selection is choosing which shots to take. A good shot is not defined by whether it goes in — it is defined by the odds before it is taken. An open catch-and-shoot three is a good shot even when it misses; a contested fadeaway is a bad shot even when it falls.

The math is simple: shots at the rim and open threes are the most efficient shots in basketball, and long contested twos are the least efficient. Great offensive players build their entire game around the first two and eliminate the third.
whyItMatters: Shot selection is the fastest way to raise a player's — and a team's — efficiency. Two players can take the same number of shots and score vastly different points per game purely based on which shots they choose. Coaches trust players who take good shots.
It also stabilizes performance. Players with disciplined shot selection do not slump as hard, because their misses are high-percentage misses that even out. Good process produces reliable results.
